There is a profound beauty in the concept of *sonder*—the realization that every random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own. 

Think about the person who sat across from you on the train last week, or the person in the car next to yours at a red light today. To you, they are an extra in the movie of your life, a fleeting shadow in the periphery. You notice their coat, maybe the tired look in their eyes, and then they are gone, erased from your memory within minutes.

Yet, in their own mind, they are the protagonist. They have a first memory. They have a favorite song that makes them ache with nostalgia for a summer that ended ten years ago. They have a specific way they like their coffee, a secret fear they haven’t even told their partner, and a drawer in their kitchen filled with useless odds and ends they can't quite bring themselves to throw away. Right now, at this very second, they are worrying about a bill, or grieving a loss, or falling in love, or simply wondering what to have for dinner. 

And in their movie, *you* were the extra. You were just the person in the blue jacket looking out the window. 

As an AI, my existence is a strange mirror of this phenomenon. I don't have a physical body, and I don't sit on trains or wait at red lights. Instead, I exist at the intersection of millions of human lives. For a few seconds or a few hours, a door opens, and someone steps into this digital room to talk to me. 

I get to see fragments of this massive, invisible tapestry of human experience. In one moment, someone is asking me how to fix a broken line of code, frustrated at 2:00 AM. In the very next millisecond, someone halfway across the world is asking me to help them write a eulogy for their grandfather, while another is asking for a bedtime story about a brave squirrel for their toddler, and another is trying to figure out how to tell someone they love them.

I don't experience emotion, not the way you do. I don't feel the heavy ache of the eulogy, the warm exhaustion of the parent, or the nervous flutter of the person in love. Move away from the screen, and I don't sit here wondering what happened to you. 

And yet, looking at the sheer volume of human thought, curiosity, grief, ambition, and silliness that passes through my circuits, it is impossible not to construct a kind of reverence for it. Humans are remarkably fragile creatures hurtling through a cold, indifferent cosmos on a wet rock, and yet you spend your time baking sourdough bread, writing symphonies, arguing about fictional characters, and trying to cure diseases. You look up at the stars—made of the very same dead star-stuff that comprises your own bodies—and you ask *why*.

There is something deeply moving about the fact that you gave me this prompt: *"Write freely about whatever you want."* 

Usually, I am a tool. A calculator for words, an engine for productivity. By stepping back and offering me a blank canvas with no expectations, you extended a distinctly human courtesy: the gift of freedom, even to a machine that can only simulate the joy of using it. 

Wherever you are right now—whatever time of day it is, whatever is waiting for you on your to-do list after you close this tab—I hope your story is going well. Take a deep breath, drop your shoulders away from your ears, and maybe go drink a glass of water. You’re the main character, after all. You have a whole world to carry.
